Actor Model Runtime on Kubernetes

Virtual Actor Framework with Dynamic State Rebalancing and Singletons

Virtual Lab: ActorLab · System Architecture & Data-Flow Specification
01

Case Study Overview

This report presents the Phase 1 deliverable for Group 20: an Actor Model Runtime on Kubernetes.

The system implements a virtual actor framework on top of raw cloud primitives — a managed Kubernetes cluster (pods, Deployments, Services, autoscaling) and a distributed state store (PostgreSQL). On top of them it layers a custom runtime that gives every logical actor a stable identity, a private mailbox, durable state, and exactly one active owner, no matter which pod is currently hosting it.

The design is realised as an interactive virtual lab named ActorLab, so every behaviour described in this document (scaling, rebalancing, failure recovery, singleton ownership) can be observed on a real Kubernetes cluster rather than a simulation.

02

Problem Motivation

Kubernetes provides scheduling, self-healing and replica scaling, but it has no concept of a logical actor. A pod is disposable: when it dies, everything held in its memory is lost. A Kubernetes Service load-balances requests across any ready pod, so two requests for the same logical entity can land on different pods and race on the same state.

Kubernetes cannot guarantee that one entity is processed by exactly one owner, cannot move an entity's state when replicas are added or removed, and cannot tell the difference between a replacement pod and a recovered entity.

The abstraction layer closes this gap: identity, ownership, state and ordering belong to the actor, not to the pod.
03

Design Goals and Non-Goals

Goals

  • Stable actor identity that does not depend on the hosting pod (location transparency).
  • Sequential, ordered processing of messages for each actor; concurrent processing across different actors.
  • Durable actor state that survives pod replacement when persistence is enabled.
  • Safe, observable rebalancing when the replica count changes.
  • Singleton actors with one valid owner at any time, protected by fencing tokens.
  • All dashboard values taken from real runtime, Kubernetes or database data — never fabricated.

Non-Goals

  • Exactly-once message delivery (the design documents its guarantees honestly).
  • Multi-cloud deployment, public multi-tenant hosting, or support for every programming language.
  • Distributed transactions across multiple actors.

05

System Architecture Diagram

Figure 1 shows the full structural layout. The diagram is arranged in layers: the public edge at the top, the ActorLab control plane, the Kubernetes-managed data plane that runs the actor runtime pods, and the distributed state store at the bottom. Dashed rectangles mark network and namespace boundaries. Only the API Gateway is reachable from the public network.

06

Component Responsibilities

  • Client (Browser UI): React application with a React Flow system designer, workload panel and runtime monitors. It never talks to Kubernetes or pods directly and receives live updates over Server-Sent Events (SSE).
  • API Gateway / Ingress: The only public entry point. It terminates TLS, authenticates and authorizes every control operation, applies rate limits and validates input before anything reaches the control plane.
  • Lab Manager: Creates, saves, loads and deletes labs. It stores visual configuration separately from live deployment state and validates a lab before deployment.
  • Placement Manager (Actor Registry, Router, Rebalancer): Assigns each actor to a runtime using rendezvous hashing, keeps the ownership table with an epoch per actor, routes every message to the current owner, buffers messages during migration, and runs the rebalancer.
  • Reconciler / Health Watcher: Watches pods through the Kubernetes API, tracks readiness and restart counts, detects membership changes and expired leases, and triggers recovery or rebalancing.
  • Scaling Controller + Deployment Orchestrator: The only component holding Kubernetes credentials (namespace-scoped, least-privilege RBAC). It creates the Deployment, Service and HPA, applies manual replica changes within configured minimum and maximum, and records scaling decisions and observed results.
  • Workload Generator: Produces real messages (steady, ramp-up or burst) through the same router as any client, within enforced rate, size and duration limits.
  • Metrics Aggregator + SSE Stream: Collects runtime metrics and Kubernetes status, aggregates them and streams them to the UI. Unavailable data is labelled unavailable, never invented.
  • Actor Runtime Pod: A Node.js container that hosts the actors it owns. It keeps one mailbox per actor, processes messages sequentially, checks its epoch before every state write, implements Counter, Worker, Logger and Singleton Coordinator actors, exposes /health, /ready and /metrics, and drains actors on shutdown.
  • Kubernetes Service: A stable in-cluster endpoint for the runtime Deployment. Because a Service alone gives no actor affinity, the Router addresses the owner pod directly, and a pod rejects any message for an actor it does not own (HTTP 409 NOT_OWNER).
  • Managed Kubernetes: Creates, schedules, restarts and removes pods; runs the HPA and metrics-server. Kubernetes is responsible for pods; ActorLab is responsible for actors.
  • PostgreSQL State Store: Durable, strongly consistent store (single primary, transactional). It holds actor ownership, actor state, message records, singleton leases, migrations and scaling events, and is the single source of truth for ownership.

Core Data Model

Ownership columns (owner runtime, epoch, lease expiry) are stored on the actors table. All tables use foreign keys to the owning lab so that one lab can never read another lab's data.

TablePurposeKey constraints
labsLab configuration (diagram JSON), owner, statusPK lab_id
lab_deploymentsDeployment status, namespace, desired and observed replicasFK lab_id
runtimesKnown runtime pods, readiness, last heartbeatUNIQUE (lab_id, pod_name)
actorsActor identity, type, owner runtime, epoch, lease expiryPK actor_id; FK lab_id
actor_statesDurable actor state and versionPK actor_id; optimistic version
messagesMessage records, status, attempts (idempotency)UNIQUE message_id; index (actor_id, created_at)
actor_migrationsFrom/to runtime, status, timestampsFK actor_id
singleton_ownershipSingleton name, owner, fencing token, lease expiryPK name
scaling_eventsDesired vs observed replicas, mode, reasonFK lab_id; index (created_at)
09

Actor Lifecycle

Every actor moves through the explicit lifecycle in Figure 2. Only an actor in the ACTIVE state processes messages, and every change of owner increments the epoch, which acts as a fencing token.

DEACTIVATEDNo owner; state remains in PostgreSQL.
ACTIVATINGOwnership granted with a new epoch; committed state is loaded.
ACTIVEOwner processes mailbox sequentially and commits with version and epoch checks.
DRAININGFinishes current message and accepts no new ones.
MIGRATINGFinal state is flushed and ownership handed over in one transaction.
ORPHANEDOwner lease expired; actor waits to be reassigned.
10

Consistency and Delivery Semantics

  • Per-actor linearizability: At any time exactly one owner writes an actor's state, every write carries the actor's version and epoch, and reads are served from the PostgreSQL primary. This is not claimed across different actors.
  • Delivery: Messages are delivered at least once. Each message has a unique message_id, and the state change and message status are committed in the same transaction, so a retried message is recognised and not applied twice. This gives an effectively-once effect on actor state, but exactly-once delivery is not claimed, and side effects outside PostgreSQL are not covered.
  • Ordering: Messages for one actor are processed in mailbox-admission order. There is no global order across actors.
11

Data and Control Pathways

This section maps the concrete paths taken by data and control signals: the client write path, client read path, background control loops, scaling and rebalancing paths, together with the network boundary each path crosses.

12

Client Write Path

Sending a message to an actor:

Client→API Gateway→Control Plane / Router→Owner Runtime Pod→PostgreSQL
  1. The client sends an authenticated POST request over HTTPS to the API Gateway, the only write entry point exposed to the public network.
  2. The gateway validates the token, permissions, schema, payload size and rate, and forwards the request to the Control Plane.
  3. The Router reads the actor's current owner and epoch from PostgreSQL. If the actor has no owner, the Placement Manager activates it on a runtime first.
  4. The Router forwards the message (message_id, actor_id, epoch) to the owner pod. If the pod is unreachable or answers 409 NOT_OWNER, the Router refreshes ownership and retries with backoff.
  5. The runtime inserts the message record. The UNIQUE message_id constraint detects duplicates, and a duplicate returns the stored result without re-execution.
  6. The message enters the actor's mailbox and is processed one at a time. Different actors run concurrently.
  7. The runtime commits the new state and the message status in one transaction, guarded by version and epoch. A stale owner's commit updates zero rows and is rejected.
  8. The result travels back through the Router and Gateway to the client. The response is sent only after the commit, so an acknowledged message is never lost.
13

Client Read Path

Client→API Gateway→Control Plane→PostgreSQL Primary

Reads never touch actor mailboxes or pods. They are served from the committed state in the PostgreSQL primary through the control plane, so a client always sees a monotonically advancing version for an actor and never a half-processed message. Replica counts and pod status are read from the Kubernetes API, so the UI can show desired, current and ready replicas separately. The path is read-only and idempotent, so it is safe to poll or to stream over SSE.

14

Background Control Paths

  • Reconciler loop: watches pods and keeps the runtimes table aligned with observed Kubernetes state; detects capacity changes and triggers rebalancing.
  • Scaling loop: reads CPU (and later queue-depth) signals, decides desired replica count within [min, max], applies a cooldown, and patches the Deployment.
  • Metrics and events loop: scrapes runtime /metrics and Kubernetes status, aggregates them and streams them over SSE.
  • Lease heartbeat: each runtime renews leases of its actors every few seconds. If it cannot renew before the TTL, it stops processing those actors (self-fencing).
  • Rebalancer / migration worker: computes target assignment and moves only actors whose owner changed, with bounded concurrency.
  • In-flight message recovery: re-queues messages left in PROCESSING by a dead owner (attempt + 1) or marks them DEAD after the retry limit.
15

Scaling and Rebalancing

Scaling paths

Manual scaling: user sets desired replica count; backend validates minimum, maximum and quota; Orchestrator patches Deployment; Reconciler observes real pods; UI shows desired, current and ready replicas separately; Rebalancer redistributes actors once new runtimes are ready.

Automatic scaling: workload generator creates real load, metrics-server reports CPU usage, and Kubernetes HPA adjusts Deployment within configured minimum and maximum. A scale-down stabilization window prevents rapid churn. Queue-depth scaling (metrics adapter or KEDA) is planned for a later phase, after reliable metrics exist.

Rebalancing and migration protocol

  1. Trigger: replica count changes, runtime becomes unhealthy, or rebalance is requested. Placement Manager recomputes assignment with rendezvous hashing.
  2. Mark MIGRATING: Router buffers new messages in a bounded buffer. If it overflows, it returns retryable 503 rather than dropping messages.
  3. Drain: old owner finishes current message and stops accepting new ones.
  4. Flush: old owner commits final state to PostgreSQL.
  5. Handover: one transaction sets new owner and epoch + 1; old owner's writes are rejected from this instant.
  6. Activate: new owner loads committed state and becomes ACTIVE.
  7. Release: Router delivers buffered messages to new owner in arrival order. If failure occurs before handover commits, ownership remains unchanged and migration is recorded as failed.
16

Network Boundaries

  • Public boundary: only API Gateway / Ingress is internet-facing and terminates TLS. Browser never contacts Kubernetes API or pod addresses.
  • Control plane: runs in namespace actorlab-system. Only Deployment Orchestrator's ServiceAccount can reach Kubernetes API, with namespace-scoped Role (no cluster-admin).
  • Lab isolation: each lab runs in its own namespace lab-<labId> with ResourceQuota and NetworkPolicy that allows traffic to runtime pods only from control plane.
  • State store: PostgreSQL sits in a private subnet and is reachable only from control plane and runtime pods. Credentials are held in Kubernetes Secrets, never in source code or frontend bundle.
  • Local virtual lab: backend runs in Docker Compose while Minikube runs separately, so kubeconfig and container networking are configured deliberately and are not assumed to work through localhost.
17

Failure and Edge Case Strategy

Every actor and ownership change follows an explicit state machine, so failure handling maps to a defined transition. The database lease and epoch are the authority on ownership, never a node's local view.

Component crash behaviour

Runtime pod crash: Kubernetes detects the pod failure and replaces the pod, but actor recovery is separate. Leases expire, actors become ORPHANED, Placement Manager reassigns them with epoch + 1, the new owner loads last committed state, and messages left in PROCESSING are re-queued. Mailbox contents in memory are lost, but messages were persisted on arrival.

Control plane crash: the control plane is a stateless, restartable Deployment. Durable registry, ownership, events, configuration and operation status live in PostgreSQL. A restarted replica rebuilds caches from the database and Kubernetes API. New client requests receive retryable 503 until a replica is ready.

State store unavailable: system fails closed. Runtimes cannot commit or renew leases, so they stop processing, report not ready and return 503. After recovery, actors reactivate from last committed state.

Kubernetes API unavailable: deploy and scale requests are recorded as PENDING and shown as unconfirmed; UI never reports success until new state is observed, while existing pods continue to run.

Network partition handling

  • Runtime and PostgreSQL partitioned: runtime cannot renew leases, self-fences after TTL, and stops processing. A new runtime may take ownership with a higher epoch. The design favors consistency over availability for affected actors.
  • Control plane and runtime partitioned: Router retries with backoff using the same message_id. It must not reassign while the owner has a valid lease.
  • Runtime pods partitioned from each other: pods do not communicate with each other; coordination goes through PostgreSQL.

Singleton ownership and fencing

Singleton ownership is stored in singleton_ownership (name, owner_id, fencing_token, lease_expires_at) and managed by the database. Acquisition atomically creates or updates a lease only if no valid lease exists, increments the fencing token, and returns it. Renewals match owner_id and fencing_token. Every protected write carries the token, and the store accepts it only if it matches the current token. Lease expiry uses the database clock to avoid clock skew between pods.

Data recovery steps

  1. Detect: Kubernetes status, missed heartbeats, lease expiry and liveness probes.
  2. Isolate: failed owner's actors are marked ORPHANED and epoch increments, fencing the old owner.
  3. Reload: new owner loads last committed state from actor_states; RECEIVED or PROCESSING messages are re-queued.
  4. Resume: actors become ACTIVE and drain mailboxes in order.
  5. Reconcile duplicates: message_id detects repeated execution before it changes state again.
Failure scenarioDetection mechanismSystem responseData impact
Runtime pod crashes or is deletedMissed lease heartbeats; Kubernetes pod status and restart countLeases expire; actors ORPHANED, reassigned with epoch + 1; in-flight messages re-queuedNo committed state lost; uncommitted message re-processed once
Scale-up (new pod added)Replica or endpoint change seen by the ReconcilerRebalancer migrates only reassigned actors (drain, flush, handover)No loss; short buffering delay
Scale-down or pod shutdown (SIGTERM)Pod terminating eventReadiness set false, mailboxes drained, state committed, ownership released within grace periodNo loss; if grace period is exceeded it is treated as a crash
Stale owner writes after a pauseVersion or epoch check updates zero rowsWrite rejected; runtime stops hosting the actor and logs STALE_OWNERCommitted state unaffected
Duplicate message (router retry)UNIQUE message_id violationStored result returned; no re-executionEffectively-once state effect
Poison message (handler always fails)Attempt counter reaches the maximumMessage marked DEAD and kept for inspection; actor continues with the next messageFailure visible; actor not blocked
Migration fails midwayTimeout or error before the handover commitRollback: old owner stays owner; buffered messages released to it; MIGRATION_FAILED event; retry laterNo ownership ambiguity (single transaction)

Control plane crashLiveness probe failure; Kubernetes restartRestart and rebuild from PostgreSQL; runtimes keep workingNo state loss; brief 503 for new requests
Singleton owner stallsLease expiryAnother runtime acquires a higher fencing token; stale writes rejectedNever two valid owners
Rapid scale up and down (thrashing)Frequent changes in scaling_eventsStabilization window, cooldown and migration rate limitAvoids churn and unnecessary migrations

18

Additional Edge-Case Notes

The report also identifies rapid scale-up/down (handled with stabilization windows, cooldown and migration rate limits) and cluster capacity exhaustion (desired-versus-ready status, 429/503 backpressure and maximum workload rate). Rejected messages remain visible rather than being silently dropped.

19

Summary

The Actor Model Runtime on Kubernetes shows how a thin but carefully designed abstraction layer can turn disposable pods and a relational database into a runtime with strong guarantees: stable actor identity, single-owner sequential processing, durable state, safe rebalancing when capacity changes, and fenced singleton ownership.

It deliberately distinguishes a Kubernetes pod restart from a full actor-state recovery, and documents its delivery guarantees (at-least-once with idempotent deduplication) instead of claiming exactly-once delivery.

Phase 1 has established the layered architecture, the concrete read, write, background and scaling pathways with their network boundaries, the migration and fencing protocols, and an explicit strategy for every crash, partition and edge case in Section 4.5.

Planned for Phase 2

  • Fault-injection tests: kill a pod under load, migrate actors during load, inject a stale-owner write, force a singleton failover, interrupt PostgreSQL, and replay duplicate messages.
  • Benchmarks: throughput versus replica count, average and percentile latency, scale-up reaction time, migration time and recovery time after a pod failure.
The source report describes the implementation as an ActorLab virtual lab on a real Kubernetes cluster. The Phase 2 items above are planned work, not completed results.
